schools.summary: Gill reads 'born of a woman' of earthly man, every descendant of Adam, but holds Job chiefly designs himself, improving his frailty into an argument with God for pity; a possible glance at Eve.

Henry unfolds the original, frailty, and pollution of life: born of Eve first in transgression, or of every man's weaker-vessel mother (partus sequitur ventrem), the life a fading flower reckoned by days.

Clarke finds a delicacy in 'Adam yelud ishah' — the first Adam lived 930 years, but woman-born Adam has few days full of rogez (tremor), born to die; Wesley: a weak, sinful creature of the sex by which sin entered.
Ellicott sets the verse at the head of the whole complaint, Job rising from his own case to the common lot, picturing the miserable creature with whom God will contend.

themes: few days and full of trouble
Eve the mother of all living

schools.summary: Gill likens the flower from the earth to man from the womb, reading Job's own history — the greatest man of the east, now easily cut down like a flower by the knife or foot.
Clarke: man as he appears is only the shadow of his real eternal being, a vegetable nipped by disease and cut down; Wesley: the flower fading, the shadow fleeting, of neither do we make account.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the misery in birth itself — woman weak, bringing forth in pain and unclean in her lying-in — so weakness, suffering, and impurity are man's portion from the womb (cf. ch. 15:14; 25:4).
Gill says the opened eyes are neither providence nor grace but rigorous justice — God set his eye on Job for evil, looked wistly and narrowly, watched every step and pursued with strictness.
Henry hears Job's plea against being brought into judgment with a God quick-sighted, holy, just, and mighty to punish, urging rather the prayer 'enter not into judgment with thy servant.'
Clarke notes that the whole chapter is directed to God alone, Job taking no notice of his friends from this point on.

themes: God opening his eyes on frail man
the speech addressed to God alone

schools.summary: Gill: no clean person can be produced from an unclean; the first man defiled all nature in him, so all born of woman are shaped in iniquity and none is pure from sin.

Clarke refers it to original and corrupt nature from which God alone can save, gathering the Chaldee, Coverdale, and Alexandrian Greek; Wesley reads 'not one' as 'no man' and hears a prayer to the prerogative of grace.

Henry: actual transgressions are the product of habitual corruption, called original sin; pleaded for compassion — 'O remember that I am flesh' — with the Chaldee that God, being one, can change the Ethiopian's skin.

Ellicott offers the alternative rendering that the verse is a wish — 'Oh, that the clean could come forth from the unclean! but none can' — beside the received statement reiterated by Bildad at ch. 25:4.

debates.question: Is the verse a flat statement of universal impurity or a wish?

sides.position: a statement — none can bring a clean thing out of an unclean
a wish — 'Oh that the clean could come forth from the unclean, but none can'

outliers.note: Proposes rendering the verse as a longing wish rather than a bare statement — 'Oh, that the clean could come forth from the unclean! but none can.'

themes: no clean thing from an unclean

schools.summary: Gregory makes the shortness of life a discipline of the righteous; the numbered months are 'recorded to be with God,' and the appointed bounds rest on the secret counsel by which God decreed all things before the ages.
Gill glosses 'determined' as 'cut out,' precisely how many days a man shall live, life being so short it is reckoned by days rather than years.
Clarke fixes the general term of life, mocking the alchemists' elixirs (all long dead), and holds the bounds apply to the race, not the individual, since folly abridges many a life.
Keil and Delitzsch turn the determined days toward the coming contrast with the tree, noting Job's 'still sadder conception of the destiny of man in death.'
Gill: not a wish that God withdraw his gracious or supporting presence, but that he turn from afflicting so extraordinarily; he notes but declines the harsher 'that he may cease' (a wish for death).

Clarke reads a hireling's breathing-time from affliction before the bound he cannot pass (cf. ch. 10:20); Wesley: withdraw the afflicting hand for present ease, till the allotted period like a hired servant's.
Ellicott renders 'accomplish' as 'have pleasure in,' the hireling rejoicing at the day his wages are paid (cf. ch. 7:2), and marks the turn to man's mortality compared to vegetable produce.

debates.question: What does 'accomplish, as an hireling, his day' mean?

sides.position: finish his day of toil / gain a respite from affliction
'have pleasure in' — rejoice at the day when his wages are paid

themes: turn from him that he may rest

schools.summary: Gill explains the botany — a felled tree whose stump is left may bud again, as the laurel or willow (though not the cypress) — set to contrast the tree's hope with man's hopelessness.

Keil and Delitzsch read the contrast at its bleakest: the tree's fate is far less hopeless than man's, for Job, a child of his age, has a still sadder conception of death, the felled man 'gone without leaving a trace of life.'

Henry grants death a removal for ever from this world — the rational soul recalled only by Omnipotence — yet insists there will be a return of man to life, resurrection being an article of Job's creed (ch. 19:26).
Clarke supplies Calmet's natural history — trees from cuttings, or long dried, revive when replanted, few failing to shoot when cut level with the earth.

debates.question: Does the tree's hope, set against man's, deny man any life beyond death, or point past it to resurrection?

sides.position: only a foil to man's hopeless ruin — the tree revives, man does not
the felled tree faintly shadows a resurrection God will surely work

themes: resurrection an article of Job's creed

schools.summary: Gill takes the aged root, dry and seemingly consumed, as the case least likely to revive, granting the tree every disadvantage before its budding overturns them.
Keil and Delitzsch read vv.8-9 as one movement toward the crushing 'how much less' of man, who dies, is broken down and melted away, and gone without a trace.
Wesley fixes the whole comparison: the stock and root 'die' only 'to outward appearance,' the tree's seeming death making its revival an apt foil to man's real death.

themes: how much less favoured is man

schools.summary: Gill lingers on 'the scent of water' — the tree buds as soon as it smells or perceives it, speedily and easily, the willow above all reviving by the benefit of water though its stock seemed dead.

Clarke calls it a fine metaphor, water acting on the perishing tree as musk or otto of roses on a swooning person; Wesley notes scent is figuratively ascribed to the tree, lending the stump a power of perception.

themes: the poetic personification of the stump

schools.summary: Gill gathers all conditions — mighty, wise, rich, honourable, and good men alike — under death, the separation of soul and body, after which the body wastes away in the grave.
Henry draws the two names, Geber the mighty who dies and Adam the earthy who gives up the ghost, tracing wasting before death, the ghost given up in death, and the awful 'where is he?' after.
Keil and Delitzsch render the Hebrew to a cheerless effect — the fallen man lies stretched out, broken down and melted away, gone without a trace of life.
Wesley answers 'where is he?' — gone to the world of spirits, into eternity, never to return; Clarke echoes the Persian Khosroo among the tombs, Fate giving back by Echo only 'Where are they?'
Gill notes the line may be read without the 'as,' a dissimilitude — the sea's waters return with the tide, but man does not return.
Clarke reads evaporation — waters drawn up yet returning as rain, the race continued though the man departs; Wesley reads a sea forsaking its place, the river drying up without hope of recovery.

Ellicott finds no particle of comparison, but contrariety — sooner will sea and rivers fail than man rise — and weighs the resurrection with care, a glimmering unexpressed longing, neither affirmed nor absolutely denied; Keil and Delitzsch keep the sterner figure of a vanishing beyond recovery.

debates.question: Does the drying water deny future life, or only return to this life?

sides.position: irrecoverable loss, no recovery
the race renewed even as the man departs (the water-cycle)
a glimmering hope refusing both flat denial and confident affirmation

outliers.note: Reads the verse as contrariety, not comparison, and catches beneath Job's bleakest words 'the glimmer of an ardent though unexpressed longing' for a life to come.

schools.summary: Gill reads the lying-down as rest in the grave as on a bed, asleep till the resurrection morn; 'till the heavens be no more' marks the term of the sleep, not its endlessness.

Clarke defends the resurrection — the words deny only reproduction like plants and return to this life, not the last-day rising, rejecting soul-sleep as 'a cold and comfortless philosophy'; Wesley: man lieth down in the grave, rising not till the general resurrection when the heavens pass away.

debates.question: Does 'riseth not till the heavens be no more' deny the resurrection?

sides.position: no — it denies only return to this life; the last-day resurrection stands

outliers.note: Insists the passage cannot be twisted to deny the bodily resurrection or to teach the soul's materiality and sleep, calling the contrary reading 'a cold and comfortless philosophy.'

schools.summary: Gill reads the wish first as a craving for shelter from present misery — the grave the house appointed for all living, or a subterraneous hiding-place from the calamities of the world.

Clarke draws a full resurrection hope, distinguishing body ('hide me') and spirit ('keep me secret'), with 'set time' and 'remember me' referring to the raising of the body; Wesley: the grave a hiding-place for the glory of a better life, the set time like Noah remembered (Gen. 8:1).

Henry hears a petition offered in pious assurance of a better life — God keeps the key of the grave to let out at the resurrection, hiding his people as treasure until the set time of their being remembered.

debates.question: Is the wish to be hidden in the grave a longing for respite from misery, or a reach toward resurrection?

sides.position: escape from present misery, the grave as shelter
a deliberate resurrection hope — the set time and God's remembering

schools.summary: Gill takes 'if a man die' as settled certainty, not doubt (the Targum restrains it to the wicked).

Keil and Delitzsch read the context at its darkest, God sealing up transgression and destroying hope; Ellicott refuses a flat denial — 'why ask the question if it were absolutely certain he would not?' — hearing an unaffirmed hope.

Clarke finds a strong persuasion of the resurrection — 'my warfare' (ch. 7:1), 'my change' as renovation, the springing again of grass (Ps. 90:5-6), an emblem of the resurrection; Wesley: he shall not live in this world, so waits till the change ends his calamities.
Henry holds both readings — the change of the resurrection (the vile body changed, Phil. 3:21, a cry of wonder) or the change at death that puts a period to his calamities.

debates.question: What is the 'change' Job waits for, and does the verse affirm resurrection?

sides.position: the resurrection / renovation — rising renewed like grass, the flesh reclothed
the change at death that ends his calamities; no life again in this world
a question that betrays a hope not yet dared, against the bleak context

themes: if a man die, shall he live again
all the days of my warfare
resurrection or the change at death

schools.summary: Gill reads the call at death (the prepared soul answering cheerfully, death no king of terrors) or at the resurrection (Christ crying to the dead as to Lazarus, the grave delivering them up).

Clarke fixes it at the resurrection — 'Awake, ye dead' — with God 'panting with desire,' yearning for the reviviscence of the sleeping dust, unable to forget the work of his hands; Wesley: God calls the soul, which cheerfully answers, loved as made and new-made by grace.

Henry gathers it into comfort against Job's darkness — a time will come when God calls and he answers, at the resurrection or at death — for grace is God's own handiwork he will not forsake but perfect (Ps. 138:8).

debates.question: Does the call sound at death or at the resurrection?

sides.position: at the resurrection, the dead called from the grave
at death, the soul summoned to God

outliers.note: Represents God himself as 'panting with desire' and 'earnestly longing for the ultimate reviviscence of the sleeping dust,' unable and unwilling to forget the work of his hands.

themes: thou shalt call and I will answer
God's desire toward the work of his hands
God yearning over the sleeping dust
grace the work of God's hands

schools.summary: Gill catches the reversal — Job, lately in a good frame with his resurrection in view, on a sudden returns to complaining of God's strict justice in numbering his steps and marking every aberration.

Henry weighs both sides: Job does right in owning sin in all his steps, but wrong in making God extreme to mark amiss, for God is not severe but punishes his people less than they deserve and blots out their sins as a cloud.

Clarke reads the particle as 'although' — although thou seemest bent on my destruction, yet thou delightest in mercy and I shall be saved — a continued hope, not a relapse; Wesley hears only 'a strict enquiry into all my actions.'
Ellicott hears a persecution so persistent it would wear out the strongest, as the mountain and rock are gradually worn away.

debates.question: Is v.16 a relapse into complaint or a continued note of hope?

sides.position: a sudden relapse into the old grievance of God's strict marking of sin
a continuation of hope — 'although thou numberest my steps, yet thou delightest in mercy and I shall be saved'

outliers.note: Reads the opening 'although,' making the verse not a relapse but a continued confidence that the God who numbers Job's steps still delights in mercy and will save him.

schools.summary: Gill offers two senses — the transgression hidden from Job himself, who cannot tell his fault, or strictly recorded, bagged and sealed like bills of indictment to be produced against him at a trial.

Clarke ties it to sealing state-transgression evidence in a bag (the 1820 'Green Bag' of parliament), or money bagged in the East — sins numbered and sealed so none is lost; Wesley: sins kept in God's memory to be brought forth, adding 'herein Job speaks rashly.'

debates.question: Does the sealed bag mean Job's sin is hidden from himself, or strictly recorded against him?

sides.position: concealed from Job, who knows not the fault he is punished for
God's exact, unforgetting record — every sin numbered, bagged, and sealed

outliers.note: Judges that in charging God with hoarding every sealed transgression 'Job speaks rashly,' the grief of the sufferer rather than the sober truth of God's dealings.

schools.summary: Gill unfolds the falling mountain that comes to nought — crumbling, withering, or dissolved — likening man, as kingdoms and great men are, to a mountain that falls by death and is never re-advanced.
Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the opening of the chapter's bleakest movement, mountain, rock, water, and flood gathered into one conclusion — 'and the hope of man thou destroyest.'

Clarke reads a lesson in mutability — mountains dashed to pieces, massive rocks removed; Wesley draws the images into one comparison, the mountain 'mouldering like a fading leaf,' ending 'thou destroyest the hope of man.'
Gill reads the waters wearing the stones into Job's own case — man, though strong as stone, is gradually worn away by the waters of affliction to the dust of death.

Clarke enriches it with proverb-lore — 'Gutta cavat lapidem non vi sed saepe cadendo,' constant dropping hollowing the flint — and reads the washed-away growth as floods destroying the grain, and so the hope of man.

themes: hope washed off like standing corn

schools.summary: Gill reads God's prevailing as absolute and final — no disease or death can be resisted, death reigning with despotic power over all men, and the prevailing 'for ever,' the grave a home never left.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the verb as seizing and grasping, not merely 'proving stronger' — God seizeth him for ever, then he passeth away — meaning the one final overpowering of death, not lifelong sufferings.

Clarke: no withstanding God, every stroke brings man down, and 'changest his countenance' alludes to covering the condemned man's face for execution (Haman, Esth. 7:8); Wesley: once life is taken it is gone for ever, sent to his long home.

debates.question: What is meant by 'thou changest his countenance'?

sides.position: the disfigurement of death upon the face
the covered face of the condemned man led out to execution

themes: sent away to his long home

schools.summary: Gill glosses the sons coming to honour — multiplied like a flock, or 'become heavy' with gold and silver, raised to grandeur — the blessing a living father rejoices in, of which the dead man knows nothing.

Clarke: the dead man is indifferent and unconscious whether his children rise or fall, for 'in that day all his thoughts perish'; Wesley: either ignorant of such events or unconcerned, a dead or dying man minds not these things.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the couplet forward with its companion, joining the sons' honour and abasement to the flesh that has pain and the soul that mourns.
Henry draws a lesson in moderating our cares — the dying man a stranger to what once filled him — since God will know what becomes of our children, to him let us commit them.

themes: the dead father knows not his sons

schools.summary: Gill offers two constructions — the dying man chastened with strong pains, too pained to heed his family, or (with Aben Ezra and the Targum) the dead man's flesh corrupting in the grave and his soul mourning over the body — leaning to the latter.

Clarke sums man's life as pain of body and distress of soul, and prefers the versions (Good, the Chaldee, Stock) that personify flesh and breath as conscious mourners — the flesh lamenting its putrefaction, the breath mourning the mouldering clay.
Henry keeps the verse with the dying man — 'dying work is hard work, dying pangs are sore pangs' — warning against deferring repentance to a death-bed and urging comforts treasured up beforehand.

debates.question: Do the pain and mourning belong to the dying man, or to his flesh and soul in the grave?

sides.position: the dying man — pain of body and distress of soul on the death-bed
the dead man's flesh corrupting and his soul/breath mourning over the corpse, personified

outliers.note: Prefers Stock's rendering in 'the daring spirit of oriental poetry,' making the flesh and the breath conscious beings — the one lamenting its putrefaction in the grave, the other mourning over the mouldering clay it once enlivened.

themes: the sum of man's life pain and sorrow
